sections.title: Can I spot two linear factors?
sections.label: Factors
sections.intro: Move all terms to one side. Look for a common factor or simple factors before using the formula.

blocks.html: If a product is zero, at least one factor equals zero.

blocks.prompt:
The quadratic expression is \(F(x)=3 x^{2} + 3 x - 36\).

Find all the real roots exactly.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite as \(\left(x + 4\right) \left(3 x - 9\right)=0\) and apply the zero-product rule.

Solve both linear factors to obtain the complete root set.

Final answer: \(\{-4, 3\}\).

sections.title: Do I lose anything by dividing by x?

Final answer: \(\{0, 6\}\).

sections.title: How do I complete the square with a leading coefficient?
sections.label: Rewrite
sections.intro: Take the leading coefficient out of the variable terms. Halve the new coefficient of x and square it.

blocks.html: Restore the constant so the new expression expands to the starting one.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=2 x^{2} - 16 x + 29\).

Write an equivalent expression in completed-square form.
blocks.solution:
Factor the leading coefficient from the quadratic and linear terms. Complete the square inside the bracket.

The horizontal offset is \(4\), yielding \(2 \left(x - 4\right)^{2} - 3\).

Final answer: \(2 \left(x - 4\right)^{2} - 3\).

sections.intro: Calculate the smallest and largest outputs at the candidates.

The graph is continuous and takes every value from \(1\) to \(163\).

sections.title: How do I recognise tangency algebraically?
sections.label: Condition
sections.intro: Set the line and curve outputs equal. Use the fact that the resulting quadratic has a repeated root.

blocks.html: A repeated root corresponds to a single common point for these line–parabola problems.

figure.alt: A tangent touches the upward parabola, while a parallel line crosses it twice.
figure.caption: A tangent touches the upward parabola, while a parallel line crosses it twice.

blocks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=2 \left(x - 5\right)^{2}\). The line has equation \(y=16 x+k\) for constant \(k\).

Find \(k\) when the line is tangent.
blocks.solution:
Equate the curve to the line. At tangency the resulting quadratic has a repeated root.

The square term is centred at \(9\). Requiring its remaining constant to vanish gives \(-112\).

Final answer: \(-112\).

sections.title: How does shifting the line change the number of intersections?
sections.label: Two crossings
sections.intro: Compare the line intercept with its value at tangency. A small sketch can confirm which direction produces two crossings.

blocks.html: A strictly positive discriminant gives two distinct intersection points.

blocks.prompt:
The curve is \(y=2 \left(x - 7\right)^{2} - 1\). The line has equation \(y=8 x+k\) for constant \(k\).

Find the intercepts k for which there are two distinct intersections.
blocks.solution:
The horizontal shift in the level must give a strictly positive squared offset.

The equation rearranges to \(2 \left(x - 9\right)^{2}=k-(-65)\) . Divide by the signed leading coefficient.

Final answer: \(k>-65\).
blocks.hint: The horizontal shift in the level must give a strictly positive squared offset.
